title: How to work any LR question
summary: Read the argument first, find the conclusion, find the gap, predict, then eliminate with a reason. One routine for all 25 questions.

slides.title: Most arguments are broken on purpose
body: Almost every Logical Reasoning stimulus is an argument: some evidence, and a conclusion the author thinks it proves. On most questions the evidence does not quite prove it. There is a gap.
Your job is to read like a skeptic. Accept every premise as true, even if it sounds false in real life, and ask only one thing: does this evidence get all the way to that conclusion?
Flaw, assumption, weaken, strengthen and evaluate questions are all questions about that same gap. Find it once, before the answers, and five question types get easier at once.
slides.callout: Accept the premises. Attack the leap from premises to conclusion.

steps.label: Read the stimulus first
steps.do: Read the whole argument before the question stem, so you read it as an argument rather than hunting for one detail.

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.do: Look for the claim everything else supports. Words like so, therefore, thus and clearly point to it; words like because, since and for point to evidence.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.do: Ask what the author took for granted to get from the evidence to the conclusion. Name it in a few words: a new term that appears only in the conclusion, a cause assumed from a correlation, a sample stretched to everyone.

steps.label: Read the stem, predict
steps.do: Now the stem tells you what to do with the gap: describe it (flaw), close it (assumption, strengthen), exploit it (weaken). Say what the right answer will roughly do before you read the choices.

steps.label: Eliminate with a reason
steps.do: Cross out each wrong choice for a reason you could say out loud: out of scope, wrong direction, too strong, describes the wrong part. Pick the survivor, not the one that sounds smartest.

slides.title: What each family does with the gap
head: Family
Question types
Your move
rows: Name the error in general terms.
Necessary Assumption, Sufficient Assumption, Strengthen, Principle (justify)
Find the missing link or make it more likely.
Find a fact that widens the gap, or the question whose answer decides it.
Must Be True, Most Strongly Supported, Must Be False, Fill in the Blank
Stay inside the text and connect what it says.
Main Conclusion, Argument Part, Method, Parallel Reasoning
Point at Issue, Point of Agreement
Find the claim both speakers address, then compare their positions on it.
Find the fact that lets both be true.
slides.note: Inference questions are the exception: their stimulus is a set of facts, not an argument, so there is no gap to find.

slides.title: Level 1: The routine on one question
slides.stimulus: Riverton's city council installed brighter streetlights on Elm Street last spring. Since then, reported bicycle thefts on Elm Street have fallen by 40 percent. Clearly, brighter lighting deters bicycle theft.
slides.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.A: Several other streets in Riverton also had their older streetlights replaced with brighter ones last spring.
choices.B: Last spring, the bicycle racks on Elm Street were moved into a staffed parking garage.
choices.C: Most bicycle thefts in Riverton take place after dark.
choices.D: Bicycle ownership in Riverton rose slightly over the past year.
choices.E: Residents of Elm Street say they feel safer walking at night than they did before.

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: “Clearly” marks it: brighter lighting deters bicycle theft. That is a causal claim.
steps.highlight: Clearly, brighter lighting deters bicycle theft.

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: After the new lights went in, thefts on Elm Street fell 40 percent. That is a before-and-after correlation.
steps.highlight: reported bicycle thefts on Elm Street have fallen by 40 percent

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: The author assumes nothing else changed on Elm Street at the same time. If something else did, the lights may have done nothing.

steps.label: Predict
steps.note: For a weaken question, look for another change last spring that would cut thefts on its own.

why.A: Says nothing about what happened to thefts on those streets, so it neither helps nor hurts.
why.B: Correct. Bikes locked in a staffed garage are hard to steal. That is another cause for the drop, which the argument overlooked.
why.C: If thefts happen after dark, lighting is more likely to matter. This strengthens.
why.D: More bikes would make a drop in thefts more impressive, if anything. It does not weaken.
why.E: How safe residents feel is not evidence about what caused the drop in bicycle thefts.

slides.title: Level 2: the routine on a strengthen question
slides.stimulus: Administrators at Tamarack Regional Hospital began a program last year in which a nurse telephones each patient two days after discharge to check on symptoms and medications. Since then, the percentage of discharged patients who return to the hospital within thirty days has dropped from 18 percent to 12 percent. The administrators conclude that the follow-up calls have lowered the rate of return visits.
slides.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the administrators' argument?

choices.A: Most of the patients who received a call said that they appreciated the nurse's concern and advice.
choices.B: Other hospitals that have tried follow-up calls found that the calls were costly to run.
choices.C: Patients who live farther from the hospital were somewhat less likely to return within thirty days.
choices.D: Nurses who made the calls reported that some patients were hard to reach by telephone.
choices.E: In the five years before the program began, the hospital's return rate stayed near 18 percent.

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: The follow-up calls lowered the return rate. This is a causal claim.
steps.highlight: the follow-up calls have lowered the rate of return visits

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: The rate fell from 18 to 12 percent after the calls began. Before-and-after.
steps.highlight: has dropped from 18 percent to 12 percent

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: Maybe the rate was already falling, or something else changed. The author assumes the drop is new.

steps.label: Predict
steps.note: A strengthener rules out a rival cause. A steady rate before the program shows the drop did not start earlier.

steps.label: Eliminate
steps.note: Drop answers about cost, mood and distance. They do not bear on what caused the drop.

why.A: Patients liking the calls is not evidence that the calls cut return visits.
why.B: Cost at other hospitals is out of scope. The argument is about whether the calls work.
why.C: Distance is irrelevant unless it changed. It gives no link between calls and returns.
why.D: If anything this weakens the case slightly, because it suggests some patients were not reached.
why.E: Correct. A flat return rate for five years makes a pre-existing downward trend unlikely, so the calls are a better explanation of the drop.

slides.title: Level 3: a necessary assumption that is easy to overstate
slides.stimulus: Park director: Dunmore Park's ranger-led night hikes, which run on Friday evenings through the summer, draw about forty visitors per outing, more than any other program the park offers. Every hike follows the same two-mile loop on the park's marked trails. The park's goal for next year is to increase the number of different people who use its trails over the course of the year. For that reason, the park should expand the night hikes from one evening a week to three.
slides.stem: The director's argument requires assuming which one of the following?

choices.A: Most of the park's visitors prefer ranger-led programs to exploring the trails on their own.
choices.B: No other program at the park draws more than thirty visitors per outing.
choices.C: Some of the people who would attend the added night hikes would not otherwise use the trails next year.
choices.D: Visitors who attend the night hikes enjoy their visits more than visitors to other programs enjoy theirs.
choices.E: Everyone who would attend the added night hikes would otherwise have stayed away from the park's trails next year.

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: Expand the night hikes to three evenings a week. It is a recommendation.
steps.highlight: the park should expand the night hikes from one evening a week to three

steps.label: Find the goal
steps.note: The goal is more different people using the trails, not more hikes or more visits.
steps.highlight: increase the number of different people who use its trails

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: Popular hikes do not guarantee new people. The extra evenings might just serve the same regulars again.

steps.label: Predict
steps.note: The plan needs at least some new faces. Use the negation test: if no one at the added hikes were new, the goal would fail.

steps.label: Name the trap
steps.note: E sounds like C but says “everyone”. A necessary assumption is the weakest link that must hold, so “some” is enough. D swaps in enjoyment for headcount.

why.A: Too strong and off the goal. The plan needs new users, not a general preference for ranger programs.
why.B: Not needed. The text already says forty is more than any other program offers; this only sets a lower cap for the others.
why.C: Correct. If none of the added attendees were new to the trails, the expansion would add no new people and the goal would fail.
why.D: Swapped concept: enjoyment is not the goal. The goal is a count of different people.
why.E: Too strong. The plan works if some of the added attendees are new. “Everyone” is not required.

slides.title: Level 4: a shifting term, one word from the right answer
slides.stimulus: Commentator: The library board has proposed using public money to buy a large set of recent novels for its spring collection. A public library's mission is to give citizens free access to information. Many recent novels can be obtained by anyone through an online subscription service that charges a monthly fee. Citizens who can obtain a book through such a service already have access to it. A library that buys copies of these novels is therefore not advancing its mission, since it is spending public money to provide something its citizens already have.
slides.stem: The commentator's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: treats being able to get a book by paying for it as the same as having free access to it
choices.B: treats being able to get a book without paying for it as the same as having access to it
choices.C: overlooks the possibility that the subscription service might raise its monthly fee
choices.D: draws a conclusion about libraries in general from the practice of a single library board
choices.E: relies on the claim that novels matter less to a library's mission than other kinds of books

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: A library that buys these novels is not advancing its mission. The reason given is that citizens already have the books.
steps.highlight: A library that buys copies of these novels is therefore not advancing its mission

steps.label: Find the mission
steps.note: The mission is free access, not just access.
steps.highlight: give citizens free access to information

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: The evidence says citizens can get the books by subscribing. The conclusion needs them to already have free access. The word “free” drops out.

steps.label: Predict
steps.note: The right answer says the argument treats paid access like free access. This is a shifting term.

steps.label: The word that kills B
steps.note: B reverses the two ideas: it says “without paying” counts as access. That is true, and not a flaw. Only A has the paid-to-free slide.

why.A: Correct. The mission is free access. The evidence shows only access at a price, yet the conclusion treats it as already met.
why.B: Reversed. Getting a book without paying does give access, so there is no error here. The argument's slip runs from paid to free.
why.C: Future fee changes are out of scope. The argument concerns what citizens have now.
why.D: The conclusion is about a library that buys these novels, not about all libraries. No generalization from one board is made.
why.E: The argument does not rank novels against other books. It says nothing on that point.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Read the stimulus before the stem.
Accept every premise; attack only the leap.
Name the gap in a few words before you look at the choices.
The stem tells you what to do with the gap.
Eliminate for a reason you can say out loud.
Inference questions have no gap: stay inside the text.
